title: Little, Fluffy Clouds
summary: Josh and Chuck explain clouds: Luke Howard's 1802 classification of clouds (cumulus, stratus, cirrus, nimbus) by shape, size and altitude, the high/mid/low level cloud families and prefixes (cirro-, alto-, strato-), how clouds form from evaporation and warm moist air meeting cooler air, condensation nuclei, precipitation types (rain, snow, sleet, freezing rain, hail), clouds' role in moving dust and regulating heat, cloud seeding, contrails, lenticular and cap clouds, mammatus clouds, noctilucent clouds and the Smith Cloud. The episode closes with a listener mail request for Frankie, who has leukemia.
topics: Royal Air Force cloud seeding disaster

segments.title: Opening banter and Luke Howard
segments.summary: The hosts joke about a chaotic producer lineup, then introduce Luke Howard, the young Englishman who renamed clouds from 'essences' and whose 1802 paper classified them.

segments.title: Four main cloud types
segments.summary: The hosts describe the basic cloud types Howard identified by shape, size, and altitude: cumulus, stratus, cirrus, and nimbus, with their Latin meanings and the Orb song named after fluffy clouds.

segments.title: High-level clouds
segments.summary: High clouds carry the prefix cirro- (cirrus, cirrocumulus, cirrostratus), with cloud bases usually 20,000 to 40,000 feet; cirrostratus can create halos around the moon.

segments.title: Mid-level clouds
segments.summary: Mid-level clouds carry the prefix alto- (altocumulus, altostratus), with bases starting around 6,000 to 20,000 feet; altostratus can darken a sunny day.

segments.title: Low-level clouds and vertical clouds
segments.summary: Low clouds include stratus that resemble fog, fair-weather cumulus, stratocumulus, and nimbostratus; cumulonimbus are thunderstorm clouds, and vertically developed clouds span multiple altitude levels.

segments.title: How clouds form and move
segments.summary: Clouds form when warm moist air meets cooler air, from evaporated surface water; fronts and condensation or freezing nuclei such as dust, sea salt, soot, and bacteria help droplets form. Clouds continuously change form as part of the water cycle.

segments.title: Precipitation types: rain, snow, sleet, freezing rain, hail
segments.summary: The hosts explain how rain, snow, sleet, freezing rain, and hail form, with hail growing in strong updrafts in severe storms until too heavy to stay aloft.

segments.title: Clouds' effects: dust, cloud seeding, and climate
segments.summary: Clouds carry dust across oceans, and particulate matter can speed precipitation, the basis of cloud seeding; the hosts cite the Royal Air Force seeding disaster in Britain and China's seeding efforts. Clouds also reflect and trap solar heat, so cloudless nights are colder.
topics: Royal Air Force cloud seeding disaster

segments.title: Unusual clouds
segments.summary: Contrails, lenticular and cap clouds, mammatus clouds, shadows cast upward in cloud, and noctilucent clouds formed after Krakatoa's 1883 eruption, with a mention of the Smith Cloud.

segments.title: Listener mail: Frankie
segments.summary: A listener writes on behalf of Brendan and his fiancée Jody, known as Frankie, who has leukemia, asking for a shout-out and a plug for the National Bone Marrow Registry.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to the website, Facebook page, and email, and mention the HowStuffWorks iPhone app.
